tagline.text: A Franciscan Baroque church on the highest ground in town

children.text: St. Bartholomew Church in Nagcarlan is a Franciscan church standing on the highest hill in town. Rebuilt in stone in 1752, it took its present form after a fire and later additions. Its four-storey bell tower and facade decorated with multicolored stones are striking, and it pairs well with the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery and Liliw as a one-day trip.
Nagcarlan is a hill town in Laguna about
97km

south of Manila. Juan de Salcedo first reached the area in 1571, and in 1578 the Franciscan missionaries Juan de Plasencia and Diego Oropesa established the parish. St. Bartholomew was the center of that mission, and it still stands on the highest ground in town, looking down over the streets. Nagcarlan is said to have become an independent pueblo in 1595, and some old houses from the 1920s and 1930s survive along Rizal Avenue, so simply walking around the church gives a feel for the old town.

The first church was built in 1583 from light materials such as nipa palm leaves and wood and was dedicated to St. Bartholomew. It is said to have been rebuilt in stone and brick in 1752 under Fr. Cristobal Torres, and townspeople reportedly donated stones and bricks of different colors to decorate the walls. A fire in 1781 destroyed part of it, and the four-storey stone bell tower was later raised under Fr. Fernando de la Puebla.

In 1845, under the supervision of Fr. Vicente Velloc, the church was extensively renovated and a choir loft supported by three arches was added. The Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery was built in the same year, and the rectory followed in 1850. In the 1990s Monsignor Jose Barrion led a major restoration.

It is not a flashy attraction, but it is a quiet church that keeps its Spanish colonial traces intact. Entry is free, and an hour is enough to see the exterior and interior properly. Combine it with the nearby Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery and the church and sandal street of neighboring Liliw for a rewarding Laguna heritage trip. A historical marker is said to have been installed at the church in 1938, so look for it near the main door. The Presidencia, close to the cemetery, is a neoclassical building from 1845 that still serves as the town hall and is worth a short walk.

The church stands at the highest point in town, and a long uphill approach leads to the main door. The semicircular arched entrance, semicircular windows and tall column pedestals show the balance typical of Baroque design. Multicolored stones and bricks offered by the townspeople decorate the outer walls.

The four-storey octagonal tower is built of volcanic tuff and brick, and its seven bells are said to bear the Franciscan coat of arms. It originally had Muslim-inspired crenellations but now wears a bell-shaped roof. Its layout is similar to the bell tower of neighboring Liliw Church, so comparing the two is fun.
The choir loft added during the 1845 expansion rests on three sturdy arches. Step inside and look up to see the sense of space that the loft and arches create.

The interior is not heavily decorated, but the gold-glowing altar, the two-tiered retablo (the decorated wall behind the altar) and the statues of saints stand out. It is dark inside even in the daytime, so let your eyes adjust slowly as you look around.

blocks.title: Holy water font, side chapel and Adoration Chapel

children.text: Inside are an old holy water font and a side chapel, and there is also said to be an Adoration Chapel for quiet prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. A side door opens onto a small courtyard. If worshippers are praying, pass quietly out of courtesy.

blocks.title: Our Lady of Lourdes beside the church

children.text: An image of Our Lady of Lourdes stands outside by the right wing of the church. Townspeople leave flowers and candles here, so you can see everyday devotion up close.

blocks.title: A pair with the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery

children.text: Around 1845, when the church was rebuilt, the Franciscans created an underground cemetery in town. Seeing the church and the cemetery on the same day connects the story of how this town was shaped. The two are about
5 minutes
apart by car.

The church is said to have served as a setting for the 1974 film Kampanerang Kuba starring Vilma Santos and for the 2005 TV drama remake starring Anne Curtis. If you like Philippine dramas, it is a good spot for a photo. Comparing the scenery on screen with the real church as you walk is another way to enjoy the town.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: The church and the underground cemetery

children.text: Leave Manila and head toward San Pablo. By car, take SLEX and the roads toward San Pablo; by bus, get off from a bus bound for Lucena or Santa Cruz.
Arrive in Nagcarlan town and walk up the approach in front of St. Bartholomew Church. Take exterior photos first and look over the bell tower and facade.
If no Mass is under way, go inside and look at the altar, the retablo and the choir loft. Also check the courtyard and the Our Lady of Lourdes image.
Go by car or tricycle to the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, listen to the guide and see the underground ossuary. It is closed on Mondays, so check the day in advance.
Have lunch at a restaurant in town. A light meal at a cafe near the cemetery also works.
Return to Manila via San Pablo.
Keep quiet during Mass and baptisms inside the church, so aim for late morning or early afternoon.

items.title: Full-day route
items.subtitle: A Nagcarlan and Liliw heritage trip

children.text: Leave Manila. A day on the Laguna heritage church route can cover several places, so an early start helps.
In Nagcarlan, see St. Bartholomew Church first and photograph the bell tower.
Look around the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery and the nearby Presidencia (the old town hall building) in the old part of town.
Eat lunch in town and rest.
Head to Liliw, about 5 minutes by car, and walk around Liliw Church and the sandal street.
You can make a short stop at Bunga Falls or another nearby sight. Skip it if time is short.
Leave for Manila via San Pablo.
Liliw is said to have been a visita (dependent chapel) of Nagcarlan until it became an independent parish in 1605, so seeing both towns together makes the history flow.
From a Manila bus terminal, take a bus bound for Lucena or Santa Cruz and get off at San Pablo or Santa Cruz. Routes and fares differ by company, so check locally.
From San Pablo, a jeepney to Liliw or Nagcarlan passes the cemetery and continues into town. From Manila to San Pablo usually takes
2–3 hours
If you took a bus to Santa Cruz, you can also get off at Pagsawitan and transfer to a jeepney bound for Nagcarlan.
Travel time varies greatly with traffic. It takes longer on weekends and holidays.
Take SLEX and exit toward Laguna, then drive through San Pablo and follow the road toward Liliw to reach Nagcarlan. Check the route with a navigation app.
It is about
97km
from Manila to Nagcarlan, and about
2–3 hours
in good traffic.
Parking near the church can be tight, so ask in town where to park.
The town center, the church and the underground cemetery are close by tricycle. Negotiate the fare or check it locally.
From the church to the underground cemetery is about
5 minutes
by car, and the jeepney stop is said to be within walking distance of the church, but sources describe its exact location differently, so check locally.
Liliw is about
5 minutes
away by car.
The church is generally open all year, so weather matters more than season. Rain makes the approach and outer walls slippery and photos darker, so the dry season mornings are recommended.

The feast of St. Bartholomew is on August 24. Some local accounts give a different date, so it is best to check the parish announcement for the exact schedule. During Holy Week, pilgrimages to the old churches of Laguna continue.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The most comfortable period. Good for photos too.
Midday sun is strong, so mornings are best, and it gets crowded during Holy Week.
Roads get congested and the interior is darker. Bring an umbrella.

Most people visit as a day trip, so there is no need to stay overnight for the church. There are cafes and small eateries near the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, and heading to San Pablo or Liliw gives you more choice. Among the sights around town are Bunga Twin Falls, said to be reached by about 10 to 20 minutes by tricycle from town plus a walk of about 5 to 10 minutes. Cottages near the falls are reported at about ₱200 to 300 in 2014-2015 accounts, but no recent rate was found and it may change, so check locally.

In Nagcarlan and around Laguna, snacks such as uraro (arrowroot cookies) and puto seco are common souvenirs. In Liliw, handmade sandals are worth a look. Prices differ by shop, so check locally. A cafe near the cemetery is reported to sell baked mussels, pancit Lucban and cassava cake. Popular dishes can run out early, so it is better to have lunch a little early.
Avoid going in during Mass or a baptism, or watch quietly from the back. One blogger waited for a baptism to end and then asked for the altar lights to be turned on to take photos.
The underground cemetery is closed on Mondays and the church may also be closed, so Tuesday to Sunday is the safer choice.
It is dark inside, so a phone night mode or a fast lens helps. It is polite not to use a flash.
Avoid sleeveless tops and short pants and dress modestly. The church is still a place of worship for the faithful.
Combining the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, Liliw Church and the churches of Majayjay and Pila lets you complete the Laguna heritage church route.
To catch a jeepney you may need to walk a short way from the church, so comfortable shoes help.
If you plan to visit several places in one trip, agree on a half-day rate with the tricycle driver before you set off.
Photographing the town from the church shows how the church sits on the hill. Morning light falling on the front gives the best photos.
After the church, visit the underground cemetery once more and compare the two buildings from the same period for a deeper understanding.
Part of the church facade collapsed in February 2016, so it is best not to go near repair areas around the outer walls.
Mass times and opening hours can change, so check the parish announcement before you go.
The approach and steps are slippery on rainy days.
Refrain from taking photos and making loud noise during services.
Bring water and a hat during the hot months of March–May.
This is a heritage building, so do not touch the walls or altar or write graffiti.
An underground ossuary built by the Franciscans in the same period as the church, about
5 minutes
away by car. You can look around while listening to a guide.
A neighboring town known for its handmade sandal street and red brick church, about
5 minutes
by car. It is said to have been a dependent town of Nagcarlan until it became an independent parish in 1605.
A Laguna heritage town with surviving Spanish-era buildings and a plaza, a good addition to a church route.
The best-known of San Pablo's seven lakes, which you can visit on the way through San Pablo.
